source.title: A Nationwide Japanese Medical Claims Foundation Model: Balancing Model Scaling and Task-Specific Computational Efficiency
source.authors: N. Aratake; Taisei Tosaki; Yuji Okamoto; Eiichiro Uchino; Masaki Nakamura; Nobutomo Matsui; A. Hatakama; Yasushi Okuno

record.file_problem: The full paper and supplementary material are present. Some figure contents are flattened, so plotted values by individual split and label count are not available as readable numbers.
record.tranche_reason: The study measures pretraining test loss across model sizes and downstream performance in a new setting: structured Japanese medical claims data. It does not reproduce language-model scaling experiments or test compute-optimal parameter/token allocation.
record.gate_note: The paper cites NLP scaling laws and reports its own test loss across five model sizes, plus downstream AUPRC across model sizes. It does not fit power laws, test small-run extrapolation, or sweep training tokens and compute to find an optimal allocation. Detailed figure traces by split and label count are not readable as numerical values in the supplied text.
record.test_reason: Pretrains encoder-only Transformers at five sizes (2.2M–101M) on structured medical-code sequences. It reports held-out MLM test loss per size and downstream AUPRC per size, a new-setting result bearing on V5 and V6. It fits no power law and sweeps neither tokens nor compute, so V1–V4 and V7 are not tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors add that, unlike the monotonically decreasing pretraining loss, downstream benefit of scale is task-dependent, and that task-optimal models beat LGBM.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses masked prediction of structured medical codes and ages in claims data, with five encoder-only Transformer sizes and reports test loss across parameter counts. It does not use text next-token loss or sweep training tokens and compute to fit scaling laws or find compute-optimal allocations.
record.method_sensitivity: Downstream performance and the optimal model size varied by task type; the paper also reports variations across fine-tuned dataset splits. Pretraining learning rates were selected separately for model sizes, but the study does not test how fitting or setup choices change scaling exponents.
record.problems: Only five model sizes and one structured medical claims dataset are tested. The study does not fit or compare power-law forms, test extrapolation, or examine data/token scaling. Downstream plot values are not numerically stated in the text, and the authors note no external or prospective validation.
record.rows_left_out: The per-split, per-label-count AUPRC traces in Fig. 5 and the supplementary plots are not entered separately because their numerical values are not readable in the supplied flattened figure text. The explicit task-level results described in the text are recorded in R6–R7.

untested.parts: No power-law fit. Data and token scaling and compute-optimal sweeps are absent. Only one structured-claims dataset and the MLM objective are used; no image, video, repeated-data or transfer regimes.
No quantitative fit of downstream performance against scale or against pretraining loss; only plotted per-split curves and text summaries.

missing.what: AUROC results across model sizes (Fig. S2) and per-size AUPRC values for each task and label count; only aggregate text summaries are recorded.

record.verdict_notes: The pretraining loss is an unweighted sum of two cross-entropies and an age MSE, not a pure log-likelihood. The larger models also needed lower learning rates after early overfitting at the default rates. Both points weaken direct comparison with V1-style laws. Data size was fixed, so the larger models may be data-limited.

versions.untested_parts: The study uses structured medical claims data rather than language models and does not test held-out language-model loss against parameters, tokens, or compute.
No power-law fit from small runs or prediction of much larger runs is reported.
No fixed-compute sweep or loss-minimising parameter/token allocation is tested.
Depth, width, and other architecture choices are not compared at fixed parameter count; layers and attention heads are fixed.

The study tests model-size scaling in structured medical claims pretraining, but does not establish a power-law fit, test other modalities such as image or video, or test repeated-data training, fine-tuning, or transfer as scaling regimes.
The study measures downstream AUPRC across model sizes for four medical prediction tasks. It does not test whether downstream performance can be predicted from pretraining loss.
The study does not compare fitting methods, parameter-counting choices, data setups, or training schedules to determine their effects on exponents or compute-optimal allocations.

rows.subject: Encoder-only Transformer, 2.16M parameters
rows.operation_detail: Measured MLM test loss across five model sizes.
rows.note: The reported test loss is part of a decreasing sequence across model sizes, but the study does not fit a power law.
rows.check: This is the smallest model, the reference point of the series, so it shows no effect on its own. GFLOPs are per forward/backward pass, not total training compute.

rows.subject: Encoder-only Transformer, 4.65M parameters
rows.operation_detail: Measured MLM test loss across five model sizes.
rows.note: The loss is lower than for the preceding model size; no power-law fit is reported.
rows.check: Small drop (8.22→7.88) for a 2.2x parameter increase, then a much larger drop at 11M. The irregular steps are not a clean power law. Loss is a summed CE+CE+MSE objective, and learning rate differs by size.

rows.subject: Encoder-only Transformer, 11.40M parameters
rows.operation_detail: Measured MLM test loss across five model sizes.
rows.note: The loss is lower than for the preceding model size; no power-law fit is reported.
rows.check: Large drop (7.88→6.10). Same caveats on loss composition and size-specific learning rates.

rows.subject: Encoder-only Transformer, 31.97M parameters
rows.operation_detail: Measured MLM test loss across five model sizes.
rows.note: The loss is lower than for the preceding model size; no power-law fit is reported.
rows.check: Small drop (6.10→5.93) for a 2.8x parameter increase. The curve flattens after 11M.

rows.subject: Encoder-only Transformer, 101.43M parameters
rows.operation_detail: Measured MLM test loss across five model sizes.
rows.note: The loss is lower than for the preceding model size; no power-law fit is reported.
rows.check: Small drop (5.93→5.74) for a 3.2x parameter increase. The decrease is monotonic but no power-law fit is reported.

rows.subject: Encoder-only Transformer task-optimal model, 32M or 101M
rows.operation_detail: Evaluated downstream one-year disease prediction across model sizes.

conditions.value: Primary hypertension and chronic kidney disease
100, 500, and 1,000 labeled patients; three dataset realizations

rows.value: The 32M or 101M model was optimal for disease prediction; task-optimal models consistently outperformed LGBM in AUPRC.
rows.note: The paper reports the disease-task optimum in aggregate as 32M or 101M and notes variation across fine-tuned dataset splits; it does not give numerical AUPRC values in the text.
rows.check: The optimum is 32M in some splits and 101M in others, so the gain from scale is not monotonic or clearly predictable. The LGBM comparison is the task-optimal model against another method, not a scaling baseline, so the baseline should be the smaller pretrained sizes. No numeric AUPRC is given.

source_check.locator_found: Sections III.D, IV.A–C and V.D; Fig. 5.

rows.subject: Encoder-only Transformer task-optimal model, 11M
rows.operation_detail: Evaluated downstream one-year medication-initiation prediction across model sizes.

conditions.value: 100, 500, and 1,000 labeled patients; three dataset realizations

rows.value: The 11M model was optimal for medication prediction; task-optimal models consistently outperformed LGBM in AUPRC.
rows.note: The text says medication prediction saturated at 11M. Scaling to 101M increased pretraining time from 53.9 h to 232.2 h without further AUPRC improvement for these tasks.
rows.check: No AUPRC gain beyond 11M (11M→101M) for the medication tasks, while pretraining loss kept falling (6.10→5.74). The LGBM baseline is not a scaling baseline.

source_check.locator_found: Sections III.D, IV.A–C and V.D; Table II; Fig. 5; Section VI.

relationships.condition: Structured Japanese claims MLM, 2.2M–101M parameters, fixed data
relationships.reason: Test loss falls monotonically (8.22→5.74), but the steps are irregular (big drop at 4.7M→11M, flattening after) and no power law is fitted (R2–R5).
relationships.display_finding: Test loss decreased from 8.22 to 5.74, with a large drop between 4.7M and 11M parameters followed by flattening, without a power-law fit.

source_check.condition: Structured Japanese claims MLM, 2.2M–101M parameters, fixed data
source_check.reason: Table II establishes decreasing loss, but the study neither fits nor evaluates a power-law form. Uneven loss reductions across uneven parameter increments do not establish departure from a power law; the untested form cannot justify limits_scope.

relationships.reason: Larger models (32M/101M) were best, but the optimum varied between 32M and 101M across splits, so gains are not cleanly monotonic (R6).
relationships.display_finding: The best model alternated between 32M and 101M across splits, preventing a consistently monotonic size trend.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.reason: Section V.D reports split-dependent performance and disease-task optima at 32M or 101M. Larger models benefit these tasks, but a uniformly optimal largest model is not established.

relationships.reason: AUPRC saturated at 11M with no gain at 32M/101M, despite lower pretraining loss, as the authors state explicitly (R7).
relationships.display_finding: AUPRC saturated at 11M parameters, with no gains at 32M or 101M despite lower pretraining loss.
